transcript_header:
Date: 2028-10-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Jonas Patel (Redwood); Alex Moreno, Priya Desai, Samir Kahn (Verdigris)
Recording: Yes
Notes: partner discovery for hybrid GPU onramp, integration patterns, compliance and pilot framing
summary: Introductory discovery between Redwood and Verdigris to explore hybrid GPU onramp integration. Key themes: routing and capacity for channel customers, private VPC/on-prem connectors, KMS integration, SLA expectations, and a proposed 48h benchmark pilot. Agreed next steps: share docs, run benchmarks, schedule network deep dive.
transcript: 00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
00:03 Alex Moreno: Yep, loud and clear — thanks Maya, excited to chat about this.
00:08 Maya Chen: Quick intros, I'm Maya, account exec at Redwood. Jonas with me, he runs infra and perf for partner integrations.
00:15 Jonas Patel: Hi all, nice to meet you. I'll mostly talk through the serving/runtime side and benchmarks.
00:22 Priya Desai: Priya here, I'm the infra lead at Verdigris. We're exploring partners to help onramp our channel customers to GPU capacity, esp hybrid setups.
00:30 Samir Kahn: Samir, BD. We're interested in speed to market and how this integrates into our reseller offering.

00:37 Maya Chen: Great. High level — Redwood provides a unified inference runtime that can be hosted, dedicated reserved pools, or private — VPC and on-prem. For partners like you we usually propose an onramp that lets customers pick hosted or bring-your-own GPU via routing policies.

00:54 Alex Moreno: When you say onramp, is that more like marketplace integration or direct channel routing? We have a bunch of resellers who want predictable pricing and a way to route traffic to their preferred infra.

01:05 Jonas Patel: Good question — both patterns are possible. We do a channel routing layer: policy-based routing by latency/cost/region. For partners you could surface a pool of partner capacity that receives traffic when selected. Fallbacks exist to Redwood hosted variants.
01:22 Priya Desai: How does networking look? We need VPC peering and we're strict about ingress — can't expose management plane to the public internet. Any air-gap or private control plane options?

01:34 Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Private supports private control plane and an on-prem package. You can run the control plane in a customer VPC, and the inference nodes talk over private peering. We also support customer-managed KMS/HSM for keys.
01:48 Alex Moreno: Ok, SOC two — are you SOC two certified? And how about logs for audits? Our compliance team will want audit trails per request.

01:57 Jonas Patel: We are SOC 2 Type II, and we provide detailed request-level audit logs. Small caveat — sometimes field names in exports differ per infra, but we can standardize. We'll share our security summary.
02:09 Samir Kahn: From a commercial POV, what's the pricing model for partner pools? Is it committed monthly or usage based?

02:17 Maya Chen: There are a few options — reserved capacity with commits for predictable throughput, or usage-based with burst. Partners often combine reserved baseline plus burst credits for spikes.

02:27 Priya Desai: Our main constraints: we need 99.9% uptime for resellers, predictable latency under 200ms p50 for short text generation, and cost targets below $0.0008 per token equivalent for our entry-tier customers. Can you meet that?

02:43 Jonas Patel: 200ms p50 is achievable depending on model and sequence length. For the cost target, quantized models + batching and KV cache can get you much lower unit costs. We'll need to run workload-specific benchmarks to confirm.
03:00 Alex Moreno: Can Redwood route to partner GPU types? We resell both Nvidia A100 and a custom ARM-based accelerator from a vendor we work with — like a hybrid mix.

03:12 Jonas Patel: We support multiple hardware families. The runtime has kernel selection and quantization paths — we can onboard model variants per hardware. For uncommon accelerators we'll need an integration window to validate kernels and throughput.
03:25 Priya Desai: What's required from our side to run a pilot? Network diagram? access?

03:30 Maya Chen: Ideally: network diagram, sample customer workloads, and a window for peering. Jonas will run a 48h mixed workload benchmark on an instance pool you select. We'll also propose an SOW for integrations and support tiers.
03:44 Samir Kahn: How long does onramp integration usually take?

03:47 Jonas Patel: For a standard VPC peering + partner pool it's typically 3-6 weeks end-to-end — less if customers accept hosted fallback while we validate. For custom kernel work on new accelerators it's longer, could be 8-12 weeks.
03:59 Alex Moreno: Security — KMS integration. We need Redwood to work with our KMS and not store keys in Redwood-managed HSM. Is that possible?
04:07 Maya Chen: Yes, we can integrate with customer KMS via key wrapping and bring-your-own-key. We also support HSM via partner integrations, we will send a KMS integration checklist.
04:19 Priya Desai: Any gotchas around egress or data residency? Some of our enterprise customers require data never leave EU. Can you pin region?

04:27 Jonas Patel: We support regional pinning and regional capacity. For strict residency we'll propose a dedicated region-based pool or a private deployment. There are networking and latency trade-offs but it's doable.

04:38 Maya Chen: Quick note on terminology — sometimes our auto transcription calls the product Redwood Dedicate or Redwood Private as 'Redwood Dedicate' — apologies if docs vary, we'll standardize naming in the deck we send.
04:47 Alex Moreno: Ha, yeah we'll let the legal team sort the spelling. On the benchmark you mentioned — what metrics will you run?

04:53 Jonas Patel: We'll run p50/p90/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, memory footprint, and cost-per-token estimated from real SKU pricing. We'll run two workload profiles: short completion bursts and longer context generation.
05:05 Priya Desai: For longer context — we care about KV cache handling across requests, especially for chat sessions, is that supported?
05:12 Jonas Patel: Yes, we have KV cache management and prefix caching. For partner pools we can tune cache TTL and eviction policies per workload.
05:20 Samir Kahn: What's the fault-handling? If partner pool runs out, do you fail requests or route to hosted variants?

05:27 Maya Chen: We support fallback policies — you can choose hard-fail, degrade to smaller model, or transparently reroute to Redwood hosted model. Many partners choose a degrade+notify strategy to maintain availability.
05:38 Alex Moreno: Regarding the SOW — what does the onboarding cost look like and are there training sessions for our support org?

05:45 Maya Chen: Onboarding typically includes integration hours (networking, SSO/KMS), a pilot bench cost, and optional white-glove runbooks. We'll include a training block for support and recording access.
05:55 Priya Desai: We use SAML SSO, RBAC is important — can we map our groups to Redwood roles?
06:01 Jonas Patel: Yes, we support SAML/SSO and group-based RBAC. We can map groups to roles and provide per-route permissions.
06:09 Alex Moreno: Any restrictions on multi-tenancy inside a partner pool? Our resellers want logical separation per customer.
06:15 Maya Chen: We support tenant isolation via route-level separation and token scoping. For stronger guarantees, we can provide dedicated pods per tenant under a reserved plan.
06:24 Samir Kahn: Let's talk timeline — we want to soft-launch a pilot to two key resellers in Q4. Is that realistic?
06:31 Maya Chen: If we start now, yes. Pilot framing: week 1 network prep and peering, week 2-3 integration and test, week 4-6 pilot traffic and monitoring. So a Q4 soft launch is feasible.
06:42 Priya Desai: Monitoring — do you expose Prometheus metrics or do we ingest through your console?
06:47 Jonas Patel: Both. We export Prometheus metrics and have per-route dashboards in Redwood Console. We can also push alerts into your PagerDuty.
06:55 Alex Moreno: For the benchmark we'd like the raw results and a spreadsheet to show our execs. Can that be exported?
07:00 Jonas Patel: Absolutely — we'll provide the raw traces, CSV metrics, and a summary slide deck.
07:06 Maya Chen: I'll send the partnership deck and security summary after the call. Jonas will schedule the benchmark run — we typically run a 48h mixed workload and share the spreadsheet.
07:15 Alex Moreno: Anything else folks need from us right now?
07:18 Priya Desai: I'll share a network diagram and list of resellers we want in the pilot. Also our preferred maintenance window for peering — weekday nights PST.
07:26 Samir Kahn: I'll sync commercial priorities and expected uplift numbers, plus a draft reseller one-pager we use.
07:32 Maya Chen: Great — recap of next steps: share docs and SOW draft, run 48h benchmark, schedule network deep dive. We'll aim to reconvene in ~2 weeks.
07:42 Alex Moreno: Sounds good — thanks Maya, thanks Jonas. Looking forward to the benchmark results.
07:46 Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs. Bye for now.
07:50 [call ends]
25:00 [note: long pauses and side conversations redacted]
30:12 Jonas Patel: (off recording whisper) we'll need to check kernel support for that ARM accelerator — not a guarantee but we can prototype with a shim layer.
31:05 Maya Chen: (typing) sending the security zip now — do you have an approved transfer method?
31:10 Priya Desai: We'll accept SFTP or a signed presigned S3 link restricted to our corp IPs.
45:00 Alex Moreno: If the pilot meets the p50 and cost targets, what's the path to GA and volume commitments?
45:08 Maya Chen: We usually draft a commercial appendix with committed baseline, onboarding credits, and a rollback plan. We can model three commitment tiers and thresholds.
52:33 Priya Desai: One last question — are there any performance regressions we should expect during model upgrades? We need guardrails for regressions.
52:41 Jonas Patel: We have rollout tooling with canary deploys and automatic fallback. Also quality monitoring tied to prompt sets so we can detect regressions and auto-roll back.
60:30 Maya Chen: Thanks again everyone — we'll follow up with the SOW and schedule. End call.
